newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Grain - Japan seen holding back on U.S. corn.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grain - Japan seen holding back on U.S. corn.

text.p: Japanese traders will be reluctant corn buyers this week and may wait for further drops in U.S. crop premiums and trans-Pacific freight rates before jumping back into the market, traders said on Monday.

"U.S. corn premiums have been gradually easing since late last month in line with downward corrections in the CBOT corn market. We'd like to wait for further drops iu premiums," a senior corn trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
Japanese importers said they had covered over 50 percent of their U.S. corn requirements for January to March 1997 shipment.
U.S. Gulf/Japan freight rates are being quoted at about $22 a tonne for the October/December period, traders said.
"Some quotes for nearby freight are slightly below $20. I'd like to see a clear direction in freight rates before I start buying," another corn trader said.
Tokyo dealers quoted U.S. corn premiums at between 99 to 101 U.S. cents a bushel C&F over Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) March futures, against nearly 103 cents two week ago.
In the oilseeds market, Japanese traders said they had already bought up to 80 percent of their U.S. soybean requirements for October shipment.
"We're gradually buying U.S. crop for November," a soybean trader at another trade house said.
U.S. soybean premiums were quoted at about 120 U.S. cents a bushel C&F over the CBOT November contract and 114 to 115 cents over January futures, traders said.
In South Korea, grain buyers are seen returning to the market after a month-long summer holiday and will probably seek more corn and by-products for feed ingredients, traders said.

Interest in South American grains and oilseeds has perked up just as South Korean President Kim Young-sam has embarked on a tour of Latin American countries to promote South Korean trade and investment.
Leaders of South Korea's major corn buyer groups are accompanying Kim, who is now in Argentina and will visit Brazil between September 10-12.
(With a contribution from Jae Hur in Seoul)

The Korea Feed Association is expected to seek 35,000 tonnes of feed corn and 15,000 tonnes of feed barley on Wednesday and several buyers are also looking for 8,000 tonnes of cottonseed meal and 12,500 tonnes of rapeseed meal on Tuesday, they said.
Local buyers were becoming more interested in Argentine corn over U.S. origin because of the more attractive prices and quality, dealers said.

"Argentine corn is getting more competitive in terms of price and quality. It is currently quoted about $10 (a tonne) lower than that of U.S. origin," a senior official at the National Livestock Cooperative Federation (NLCF) said.
South Korea's state-backed NLCF bought a total of 157,000 tonnes of Argentine corn last week.

Market talk was also circulating that the NLCF had bought 40,000 tonnes of Brazilean soymeal at $299 a tonne C&F from Daewoo International for shipment from March 1-20, though this could not be confirmed.
Traders said the NLCF was additionally expected to buy one or two cargoes of Argentine corn this week.
